title: GPU shape benchmark results (Dedicated) — v2025-03-05
content:
Context
- Purpose: provide a consistent, apples-to-apples comparison of Redwood Dedicated “shapes” across representative workloads (short/long context, streaming) to inform:
  (a) tier→shape mapping, (b) perf floors / expectations, (c) capacity planning headroom assumptions.
- Audience: Infra/Fleet, SRE, Product Dedicated, Finance.
- IMPORTANT: these numbers are for internal sizing + catalog guidance. Not customer-facing; perf varies by model version, quant profile, batching, and request mix.

Benchmark setup (common)
- Runtime: Redwood Inference Engine (RIE) v0.19.3
- CUDA/driver: 12.4 / 550.xx (fleet baseline at time of test)
- TensorRT-LLM kernels enabled where supported; flash-attn v3 enabled
- Prefill+decode: continuous batching ON; prefix/KV cache ON unless explicitly noted
- Target: stable “sustained” numbers over 20 min runs after warmup (first 3 minutes discarded)
- Metrics captured: 
  - output_tok_s_p50/p95: aggregate output tokens/sec at the deployment (all GPUs)
  - ttft_ms_p50/p95: time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming endpoints, otherwise time-to-first-byte (TTFB)
  - notes include common bottlenecks observed
- Regions used (where available): us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-central-1

Workloads (standardized)
- W1 chat-short (non-stream)
  - prompt_in: 512 tokens, max_out: 256 tokens
  - typical concurrency target: 16–64 depending on model/shape
- W2 chat-longctx-8k (non-stream)
  - prompt_in: 8192 tokens, max_out: 512 tokens
- W3 summarize-32k (non-stream)
  - prompt_in: 32768 tokens, max_out: 256 tokens
- W4 chat-short-streaming (stream)
  - prompt_in: 2048 tokens, max_out: 512 tokens, SSE streaming
  - note: TTFT is the primary customer-perceived latency metric; tokens/sec is still useful for capacity
- W5 embeddings-batch (non-stream)
  - input: 512 tokens avg, batcher enabled; report req/s and p95 latency

Models tested (representative)
- M1 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (FP16)
- M2 Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (FP8 where supported; otherwise INT8 weight-only or FP16 noted)
- M3 Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct (INT8 weight-only)
- M4 BGE-large-en-v1.5 (embeddings; FP16)

Shape naming (internal)
- h100-sxm-80gb-8 (NVLink) = 8×H100 SXM 80GB
- h100-pcie-80gb-8 (PCIe) = 8×H100 PCIe 80GB
- a100-sxm-80gb-8 (NVLink) = 8×A100 SXM 80GB
- l40s-48gb-8 (PCIe) = 8×L40S 48GB
- a100-sxm-80gb-4 (NVLink) = 4×A100 SXM 80GB

TAB: SUMMARY (normalized results)
- Interpretation: for each (shape, model, workload) row, concurrency was tuned to hit ~70–85% GPU utilization without runaway queuing.
- Where two quant profiles exist, we used the Redwood catalog default for Dedicated (notes indicate deviations).

Notes on variance drivers (what moved numbers >5–10%)
1) Streaming accounting & metric attribution
- Prior to github://redwood/pr-19422, some harness views double-counted tokens for certain streaming paths (client retries + chunk flush). This impacted displayed tok/s but not actual runtime performance. Ensure dashboards use post-fix metric names/labels.

2) Prompt length distribution (especially longctx)
- W2/W3 are extremely sensitive to actual prompt tokenization variance (JSON escaping, tool call schemas, etc). p95 TTFT tails widen rapidly with a small % of 12k–16k “outliers”.

3) Host CPU + networking
- For very high concurrency (8B on H100; embeddings batch), tokenization and gateway fanout can become the bottleneck.
- Symptom: GPU util dips while p95 latency rises; fixing requires CPU pinning / larger host shape / gateway tuning.

4) Quant profile differences
- FP8 (H100) vs INT8 weight-only (A100) is not a simple multiplier; kernels differ and prefill/decode balance shifts.
- For 70B, A100 INT8 W-only showed notably worse TTFT at long contexts than expected from pure compute ratios.

5) Interconnect (SXM NVLink vs PCIe)
- Multi-GPU sharding + KV movement patterns can make PCIe shapes underperform disproportionately for longctx.
- Largest observed gap: ~10–18% on W2/W3 depending on model.

6) Thermal/power management / clock drift
- A few runs on l40s-48gb-8 showed clock variability under sustained load; tok/s stddev increased. Fleet should confirm power caps and cooling baselines for Dedicated pools.

7) Cache hit rate / prefix reuse
- Our standardized harness uses low prefix reuse by design (to avoid “cheating”). Real customer workloads with repeated system prompts often see better effective throughput due to prefix caching.
- For SLO semantics, we should be careful: caching improves serviceability but should not be required to meet the committed floor.

Preliminary guidance (for catalog + tier mapping discussions)
- h100-sxm-80gb-8: preferred for Premium (longctx + strict TTFT/streaming) and for 70B heavy workloads.
- h100-pcie-80gb-8: acceptable for Plus/Premium where NVLink supply constrained, but expect slightly worse p95 TTFT and lower tok/s; price accordingly.
- a100-sxm-80gb-8: viable for Standard/Plus for 70B moderate ctx (<=8k) and strong for mixtral/8B workloads.
- l40s-48gb-8: good for cost-sensitive tiers and mid-size models; avoid positioning for 70B, and caution on longctx-heavy mixes.
- a100-sxm-80gb-4: “small commit” option; best for non-longctx and lower concurrency. Needs stricter admission control to protect p95.

Open questions / TODO
- Add runs for:
  - a100-sxm-80gb-8 w/ alternative quant profiles (where quality allows)
  - h100-sxm-80gb-4 (if we want a smaller Premium shape)
  - 32k context on mixtral (if catalog wants to claim it)
- Standardize harness to record CPU util and gateway metrics per run (to separate GPU vs host bottlenecks).
- Align with SRE on which exact metric label(s) map to the Dedicated throughput SLO (see ADR-027 + ENG-19244).
